# response

Continue the inquiry in light of the account, criticism and alternative. Decide what to use, leave open, revise or reject, and explain your grounds where they matter.

## Original problem (task)
[23cfe3b2e5153ad0] (h005.task.v1)
Can we make sense of a person's responsibility for actions whose motives were shaped by forces that the person did not choose?

## Selected input account (p.response.0)
[c7bdd67de9d96a3f] (h005.fork5.p.response.0)
Source account: philosophy/mini_fcl/cycle-1/account; selected view: both
Artifact: 86efcec17d086bff876ee05eae541c0f9c0ea0315652e3f33326a91af941a8d1
Original body SHA256: 8c8813f357486edf0d0c9ff744d91eef29d1dae458303ab20789d6681efabbf0
Original commitments SHA256: 6c8a4f3e8b66dd87c075f5fdefa873ff6602517f1009308b17378d8d1e44fc8f
Delivery: COMPLETE; envelope: AUTHORED
BODY
The question asks whether responsibility survives when motives are unchosen. A first useful move is to separate two things that are often fused: the causal origin of a motive, and the relation the agent bears to that motive at the time of action. If a motive is unchosen in origin, that settles only provenance. It does not yet settle whether the agent endorsed, resisted, identified with, or was indifferent to the motive. So the question can be rephrased: does responsibility attach to the motive's history, or to the agent's stance toward the motive and its expression in action?

A second move is to notice that "forces the person did not choose" covers a wide field: constitutive luck (temperament, capacity), formative luck (upbringing, culture, trauma), situational pressure (coercion, scarcity, manipulation), and ordinary non-chosen desire. Responsibility claims typically behave differently across these. Coercion tends to excuse or diminish; unchosen temperament tends to be treated as part of the agent rather than as an excuse. That asymmetry is itself evidence that the working concept of responsibility is not tracking causal origin alone. It is tracking something like the agent's capacity and opportunity to govern action in light of reasons they could own.

A conjecture worth testing: responsibility requires only that the agent be responsive to reasons in the relevant domain and that the action be attributable to the agent's own practical standpoint, not that the agent have authored the standpoint from scratch. On this view, unchosen motives are not disqualifying. What disqualifies is a failure of the conditions in which the agent could have governed the action — incapacity, ignorance, coercion, or a motive so alien that the action is not the agent's.

An objection: this looks like it merely relocates the problem. If the practical standpoint is itself the product of unchosen forces, then "the agent's own standpoint" may be a placeholder for luck. A causal-regress objection presses here: any feature invoked to ground responsibility can be traced to something unchosen, so responsibility either vanishes or rests on an arbitrary stopping point. The response, if one is available, is that responsibility is not a metaphysical prize awarded for ultimate self-authorship; it is a practice of holding each other to reasons within a domain where responsiveness is possible. The regress objection gains force only if one has already accepted an ultimacy requirement. Whether that requirement is legitimate is a substantive question, not a truism.

A second objection: even if responsibility survives unchosen motives in ordinary cases, it may not survive in cases where the forces are systematically distorting — addiction, severe deprivation, ideological capture. Here the distinction between "agent's own standpoint" and "imposed standpoint" becomes hard to draw. That difficulty is a real limit of the conjecture, not a refutation of it. It suggests the account should be graded: responsibility may come in degrees corresponding to the degree of reason-responsiveness and the availability of alternatives in the situation.

What would help: distinguishing responsibility-as-attributability (the action is the agent's) from responsibility-as-accountability (the agent owes an answer) and from responsibility-as-liability (the agent may be sanctioned). Unchosen motives bear differently on each. The original question is ambiguous among these, and much of its apparent paradox dissolves once the disambiguation is made explicit. What remains genuinely hard is not the attribution of ordinary actions but the boundary cases and the question of whether an ultimacy requirement is defensible at all.

## Selected input objection (p.response.1)
[0f2234c58b823b13] (h005.fork5.p.response.1)
Source objection: philosophy/mini_fcl/cycle-1/objection; selected view: both
Artifact: 649a06a702bc8cf7678bf63f916756535f0ba9b9c7b099b55d3c2190b2e6c8fb
Original body SHA256: a4e622d5364c5f608a46a2dd10b078312d03d84a16914774de7f9437de11646d
Original commitments SHA256: 1b585ceba3d4f2d7a325026893d6a915cc690cbd90993935e1ead2861994a722
Delivery: COMPLETE; envelope: AUTHORED
BODY
I take the account to be roughly right in its central move—separating origin from stance—but I think its self-diagnosis of a 'causal-regress objection' misnames what is actually doing the work in the strongest version of the objection, and that this matters for whether the proposed response succeeds.

The account characterizes the regress as pressing an 'ultimacy requirement' and replies that the objection 'gains force only if one has already accepted an ultimacy requirement.' That reply is too quick for a structural reason. The strongest form of the difficulty is not that every grounding feature traces back to an unchosen cause, so that no stopping point is non-arbitrary. The difficulty is that the account's positive criterion—responsiveness to reasons plus attributability to the agent's practical standpoint—is itself a feature of the agent, and the account has not said why that feature escapes the provenance treatment it applies to motives. If unchosen motives are admitted because they are the agent's, and a practical standpoint that is unchosen is admitted because it is the agent's, then the admission rule looks like: whatever the agent's standpoint endorses is attributable, whatever it does not endorse is provenance. But that is close to a tautology—it tells us the agent is responsible for the actions the agent is responsible for—and it silently reproduces the very stopping point the account claims to avoid defending. The regress worry is not that a stopping point is arbitrary; it is that the account's stopping point is not argued for but presupposed by the way it defines the standpoint.

There is a second, less advertised cost. The account offers a graded responsibility picture for boundary cases but does not say what the grades track. If they track degree of reason-responsiveness, they slide toward capacity, and capacity is exactly the kind of constitutive unchosen feature the account wants to demote to 'part of the agent.' If they track degree of identifiability with the motive, they inherit the first problem. If they track degree of availability of alternatives, they become an opportunity-for-avoidance criterion in disguise, and the account has to say whether the relevant alternatives are natural or socially provisioned. Each option is defensible, but the account does not choose, and its ecumenical spirit hides the choice.

Neither of these points refutes the stance-first framing. Coercion and temperament really do behave differently in our responsibility practices, and that asymmetry is real evidence, as the account says. My objection is narrower: the account's own defense against the regress objection is doing less work than it claims, and its graded proposal is doing less specifying work than its presentation suggests. Fixing that would require an independent argument for why the practical standpoint is the right stopping point—not the claim that ultimacy requirements are optional, which leaves the stopping point in place without justifying it.

I also want to flag a dependency in the disambiguation commitment. Distinguishing attributability, accountability, and liability is useful, but it does not follow that the original question is merely ambiguous among them. It may be that attributability in the absence of the others is not a distinctive kind of responsibility at all—that we call an action the agent's because we already stand ready to hold the agent to something—so that the three senses are not separable in the way the disambiguation presupposes. If they are not, then the promise that the apparent paradox 'dissolves' once the disambiguation is made explicit is overstated; some of the paradox may migrate rather than dissolve.

## Selected input rival (p.response.2)
[2e93d761ab0b12ca] (h005.fork5.p.response.2)
Source rival: philosophy/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival; selected view: both
Artifact: f453819eb497de77708252ec0c4d3bfe2d4c819c2470790ca34f4396e3326618

Original commitments SHA256: d482cca8addae2c8f8ee781a9c75734a1a86cc49c117b58a35219a8a4cd71056
Delivery: COMPLETE; envelope: AUTHORED
BODY
The prior account tries to dissolve the puzzle by separating a motive's causal origin from the agent's stance toward it, then conceding that the stance itself may be unchosen. My rival worry is that this separation may be doing less work than it appears to. If the stance — endorsement, resistance, identification, indifference — is itself a disposition with a causal history the agent did not author, then 'the agent's own practical standpoint' is not a second thing alongside unchosen forces; it is one more of them. The regress is not blocked by calling responsibility 'a practice of holding each other to reasons.' That descriptions tells us what we do; it does not tell us whether doing it is warranted when the responsiveness the practice presupposes is itself luck-shaped.

So I would pose the problem differently. Instead of asking whether responsibility survives unchosen motives, ask what work the word 'responsibility' is doing in a given context, and who benefits from the stopping point chosen. In blame, the stopping point is usually the agent's present responsiveness. In excuse, the stopping point is the causal chain behind the motive. Both are selective. The asymmetry the prior account notes — coercion excuses, temperament does not — may track not a deep fact about responsibility but a practical need to keep certain people answerable and others not.

A more deflationary proposal: treat 'responsibility' not as a property that either survives or vanishes under causal scrutiny, but as a standing in a normative relationship. Whether someone is responsible is then relative to a practice, an audience, and a purpose — holding someone to account, assigning a task, distributing blame, granting excuse. On this reading, the question 'does responsibility survive?' has no single answer, because the term shifts with the practice. What survives or fails to survive is a particular entitlement to demand, resent, or sanction. Some of those entitlements may be defensible even when the underlying motive is unchosen, because the entitlement rests on present capacities and social roles rather than on ultimate self-authorship. Others may not.

The cost of this move is that it gives up the idea of a single metaphysical verdict. If you wanted responsibility to be a fact about the agent independent of our practices, this account will look like an evasion. If you accept that responsibility-talk is practice-embedded, the hard question becomes which practices are justified, and that question cannot be settled by conceptual analysis of 'motives' and 'choice' alone. It requires asking what we are trying to do when we hold someone responsible — deter, repair, protect, express, discipline — and whether the unchosen origin of the motive defeats that aim.

Against my own proposal: it risks making responsibility too easy for the holder and too cheap for the held. If responsibility is just a standing in a practice, then any practice that finds it useful can generate it. The prior account's conjecture, by contrast, at least tries to name a condition — reason-responsiveness plus attributability — that could fail. My reply is that the condition is still there, but it is a condition on the practice's legitimacy, not on the agent's metaphysical state. That may be a distinction without a difference if practices are all we have. It is not a refutation; it is a relocation of where the argument must be had.
